questions.prompt: What does @pytest.mark.parametrize produce from one decorated function and three value tuples?

options.text: One test that stops at the first failing tuple
Three independent tests, each reported separately
A single test that averages the results
Nothing until you also add a fixture

questions.explanation: pytest runs the function once per tuple, generating independent tests so one failing case doesn't hide the others.

questions.prompt: Match each parametrization term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Runs one test once per row of input data
Readable labels so a failure names the case
An input at the edge of valid/invalid
What stacking two parametrize decorators creates

questions.explanation: parametrize generates one test per row; ids label each case; boundary values sit at the edges; stacking decorators multiplies the cases together.

questions.prompt: Which are good uses of parametrization? Select all that apply.

options.text: Checking one behavior across many inputs
Covering boundary values (below, at, above a limit)
Merging three unrelated functions into one test_everything
Turning five near-duplicate tests into one table

questions.explanation: Parametrize the same logic over varied data (including boundaries) and remove duplication; don't force unrelated behaviors into one generic test.

questions.prompt: Inputs at the edge of valid/invalid — where off-by-one bugs live — are called ____ values.
questions.explanation: Boundary values (min, max, just-below, just-above) are prime targets for parametrized tables.

questions.prompt: Why avoid computing the 'expected' value with the same formula used by the code under test?

options.text: It makes the test file longer
The test could pass even when both the code and the formula are wrong

questions.explanation: If the test mirrors the implementation, a shared mistake passes silently; hand-written expected values are an independent check.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to collapse several near-identical tests into a parametrized one.

items.text: Spot tests that differ only in input/expected values
Write one test body and a table of (input, expected) rows
Add ids so each case is labeled in the report

questions.explanation: Identify the shared logic, extract the varying data into a table, then label the rows for readable output.
